title: Time Based Key-Value Store
pattern: sort by timestamp + binary search for the rightmost value <= query
statement:
A time-based key-value store keeps one key whose value is overwritten over time: a write stores a value together with the timestamp at which it happened. A read at timestamp `q` must serve the value that was in effect at `q`, that is the value of the write with the largest timestamp not greater than `q`.

You are given the write history as two parallel arrays: entry `i` stored `values[i]` at `times[i]`. You are also given a list of read timestamps `queries`. For every read, return the value that must be served, or `-1` if no write happened at or before that timestamp.

If two writes share the same timestamp, the one appearing later in the history is in effect, because a write overwrites whatever was stored at the same instant. Only the first `min(times.length, values.length)` entries of the history exist.

Example: `times = [1, 4, 7]`, `values = [30, 60, 90]`, `queries = [1, 5, 3, 8, 0]` returns `[30, 60, 30, 90, -1]`: at time `5` the value written at time `4` is still in effect, at time `3` the value from time `1` is, and at time `0` nothing has been written yet.

Return the answers in the order the queries were given.

Constraints: `1 <= times.length <= 200` and `0 <= times[i] <= 10000` and `1 <= values.length <= 200` and `0 <= values[i] <= 10000` and `1 <= queries.length <= 200` and `0 <= queries[i] <= 10000`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(times: number[], values: number[], queries: number[])`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: For one query the answer is the write with the largest timestamp that is still not greater than that query. Work out by hand what a query before every write must return.
Sorting the writes by timestamp turns every read into a predecessor search: the last element whose timestamp is not greater than the query.
Keep equal timestamps in their original order when sorting, so the rightmost match of the search automatically picks the write that overwrote the others.

editorial.approach: The brute force answers each query with a full scan of the history, keeping the write with the largest timestamp not greater than the query and using `>=` when comparing so that a tie is won by the later entry. That is O(n) per query. The optimal sorts the history once by `(timestamp, index)` and then answers each query with a binary search for the rightmost position whose timestamp is not greater than the query. Sorting ties by index makes that rightmost position the latest write among equal timestamps, which is exactly the overwrite rule, so no extra tie-break logic is needed after the sort. Keep `pos = -1` to mean nothing matched and emit `-1`.
editorial.why_optimal: A read is a predecessor query on the timestamps: the answer is the largest stored key not exceeding the target. Comparison-based predecessor search costs O(log n) and cannot be beaten without extra structure, and the single sort is O(n log n) against m lookups, so O(n log n + m log n) is optimal here. The stated bounds (n, m <= 200, timestamps <= 10^4) make even the scan instant, but scanning the whole version history on every read is exactly how a versioned store collapses under load.
editorial.pitfalls: Returning the *first* match on a tie instead of the last, which loses the overwrite. Searching for the smallest timestamp greater than the query (successor) instead of the largest one not exceeding it. Forgetting the empty-history case and returning a stored value instead of -1, or initializing the best timestamp to something larger than any real timestamp. Off-by-one in the binary search: `lo` may only advance past `mid` when `times[mid] <= q`, otherwise a query smaller than every timestamp returns index 0 instead of -1. And iterate only over `min(times.length, values.length)` entries, since a shorter `values` array otherwise reads `undefined` in JavaScript (or raises in Python) and corrupts the answer.
